html:
The map's label for the peoples of the Great Plains of North America who lived mainly by hunting bison, shown from 1500 BCE to 1500. This was before horses. Hunters went on foot, and dogs pulled loads on a travois, two poles tied in a V.

The great hunts drove herds over cliffs or into corrals. At Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Alberta, people did this for thousands of years. A bison gave meat, often dried and pounded into pemmican, hides for tents and robes, and bone and sinew for tools.

Along the rivers of the eastern Plains, farming villages grew up after about 900 CE, raising maize, beans and squash in the Three Sisters way, and trading with the hunters.

After this map ends, everything changed. Horses spread north from Spanish New Mexico, mostly after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 (horses on the Plains). Peoples such as the Comanche, the Lakota and the Plains Cree moved onto the Plains and became mounted bison hunters. In the 1870s and 1880s commercial hunting brought the bison close to extinction and broke their way of life.
